analysis.one_liner: Restricts credit card rate hikes, hidden fees, and billing tricks, and limits cards for people under 21.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the Senate Banking Committee and won 21 cosponsors, but the Senate never voted on it; its consumer protections instead became law that year through a House-passed credit card bill signed in May 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite credit card rules to stop common practices that cost cardholders money. It would require 45 days' notice before an interest rate increase and let the cardholder cancel the card and pay off the old balance at the old rate; it would ban "universal default" (raising your rate because you fell behind on some other bill); it would require payments to be applied to the highest-interest balance first; it would restrict over-the-limit fees, fees just for paying a bill, and interest charged on top of fees; and it would require statements to show how long and how much it takes to pay off a balance making only minimum payments. It would also bar most credit cards for people under 21 without a cosigner or proof they can repay, limit fees and expiration dates on gift cards, and mandate a study of the hidden "interchange" fees merchants pay.
analysis.who_benefits: Cardholders — especially the tens of millions who carry a balance from month to month — gain the most: fewer surprise rate increases, no retroactive rate hikes on existing balances, no penalties for on-time payments, clearer statements, and at least 21 days to pay. Young adults and students gain from restrictions on marketing cards on campus and on issuing cards to people under 21. Gift card buyers gain from limits on fees and expiration. Merchants get a government study of the hidden interchange fees they pay on every card transaction.

how_it_helps.text: Requires 45 days' advance notice before a rate increase, and lets the cardholder cancel the account and pay off the existing balance at the old rate instead of accepting the increase [S3, S4].

Bans universal default — raising your card's rate because of trouble on other debts or a dip in your credit score — and allows rate increases only in narrow cases, ending within six months unless you slip again on that same account [S3, S4].

Requires payments to be applied to the highest-interest balance first, ends double-cycle billing tricks, extends the minimum billing period from 14 to 21 days, and sets a 5 p.m. deadline standard so payments made on the due date count as on time [S3, S4].

Restricts over-the-limit fees (opt-in only, once per cycle, not when a fee itself pushes you over the limit), bars separate fees just for paying a bill, bars charging interest on top of fees, and requires late fees to be reasonably related to the issuer's cost [S3, S4].
Requires statements to show how many months and how many dollars it takes to pay off the balance at minimum payments, and what payment would clear it in 36 months [S3, S4].

Bars credit cards for people under 21 unless they have a cosigner, show independent ability to repay, or complete a certified financial literacy course, and restricts marketing affinity cards to students [S3, S4].
Bars dormancy, inactivity, and service fees on gift cards and most gift card expiration dates [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers and banks lose revenue from interest-rate increases on existing balances, universal default, over-the-limit fees, and payment fees, and face new compliance and disclosure costs. Retailers and gift card issuers lose inactivity fees and revenue from expiring card balances. To the extent issuers cannot charge these fees to risky customers, some of that cost may be passed back to all cardholders through higher rates or annual fees — a cost the bill's supporters accepted as the price of ending fee traps.
analysis.who_pays_short: Card issuers, banks, gift card sellers

drawbacks.text: Bars issuing a credit card to anyone under 21 without a cosigner over 21 who is jointly liable, proof of independent ability to repay, or a certified financial education course — which shuts out many young adults, including students and young workers, who previously could get their first card on their own [S3, S4].
The bill as reported would take effect only nine months after enactment, so cardholders would keep living under the old fee-and-rate-hike practices for close to a year after passage [S3].

The reported version also contains provisions unrelated to cardholder protection — raising the FDIC's borrowing authority from $30 billion to $100 billion, with temporary authority up to $500 billion, and the NCUA's from $100 million to $6 billion — expanding the borrowing capacity of deposit-insurance funds with little connection to credit card reform [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and broad: the fee traps, retroactive rate increases, and billing tricks this bill targets were levied on millions of ordinary cardholders, and the disclosure and payment-credit rules cost issuers little per customer. The real costs are borne by card issuers, whose fee income was the bill's target, and some of that may resurface as higher rates or annual fees spread across all customers. The under-21 restrictions are the most debatable provision, trading protection from on-campus debt marketing against reduced access to credit for young adults. On balance, the consumer gains outweigh the costs, which is why the substance of this bill became law the same year.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Banking Committee reported the bill and it sat on the Senate calendar, but the Senate never took a floor vote on it — the same protections were enacted instead by attaching this bill's language to a House-passed credit card bill, which President Obama signed on May 22, 2009.

narrative.text: Introduced on February 11, 2009 by Senator Dodd and read twice, then referred to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee [S1, S6].
Dodd introduced the bill with 21 original cosponsors — 20 of the Senate's 58 Democrats and the chamber's one Independent, Senator Sanders [S5].

On March 31, 2009 the Banking Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with amendments, and on April 29, 2009 Dodd reported it with an amendment in the nature of a substitute — a full rewrite — and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 54 [S6].
Senator Dodd filed the committee's written report on May 4, 2009 [S6].
No floor vote on S. 414 appears anywhere in the action history; the bill sat on the Senate calendar until the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cardholders did not lose out here: the substance of this bill became law the same year when the Senate attached its language to a House-passed credit card bill, which President Obama signed on May 22, 2009. The credit card industry gave up the fee practices this bill targeted, though banks found ways to recover some revenue through higher rates and annual fees on other customers.

for.name: Christopher Dodd
for.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, shepherded it through committee to a favorable report with a substitute amendment, filed the committee report, and placed it on the Senate calendar

for.name: President Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Signed the credit card protections into law in May 2009 after they were attached to a House-passed bill

against.name: Credit card issuers and banks
against.what_they_did: Opposed the new restrictions on rate increases and fees and pushed to slow the rules' effective date

sides.party_line_note: All 21 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's sole Independent; no Republican cosponsored [S5]. The committee reported the bill favorably without a recorded roll call [S6].

industries.note: The bill strips away core revenue practices: rate increases on existing balances, universal default, over-the-limit fees, fees for paying a bill, and interest charged on fees. The industry's gain from these practices came directly out of cardholders' pockets, so its interest ran against the public's in this bill.

industries.industry: Gift card and prepaid card issuers
industries.note: The bill bans dormancy, inactivity, and service fees and most expiration dates on gift cards — revenue collected largely from money consumers had already spent and forgotten. The FTC would enforce the ban [S3].

The bill does not cap the interchange fees merchants pay on every card swipe, but it directs the Comptroller General to study how those fees work, how they are priced, and how the undisclosed cost affects retail prices — the first step toward regulating them [S3, S4].

industries.industry: Deposit insurance funds (FDIC and credit unions)
industries.note: A rider unrelated to cardholder rules raises the FDIC's borrowing authority from $30 billion to $100 billion (temporarily up to $500 billion) and the NCUA's from $100 million to $6 billion, strengthening the funds that back ordinary depositors' accounts [S3].
